evidence_quotes.quote: In Kisumu’s DMM, KIWASCO delivers water in bulk to metered master-operators (either group-operators or individuals) who pay KIWASCO for the water they sell each month. The master-operators are responsible for selling water to consumers, either through piped connections to dwellings or through a network of water kiosks and standpipes for those too poor to afford private connections.

This study showed that DMM has lowered the cost of kiosk connections. Master-operators ensure that kiosk operators get connected once they have raised enough money to purchase water meters and pipes. In Manyatta B, prospective operators may have to purchase the meter and pipes, and also pay for pipe layout and connection fees.
If one kiosk operator is late with payments, the master-operator may cover his expenses for a short time so that all operators in that network will continue to receive utility water.
KIWASCO’s list of individual water-kiosk operators was used as a sampling frame. A random sample of 103 operators was interviewed in May–June 2013
In Manyatta, 73.3% reported disconnection, compared to 36.2% in Nyalenda A and 23.1% in Nyalenda B.
Nyalenda A and B prices were found to be lower than Manyatta prices. On average, a 20 l jerrican in Nyalenda A costs 2.97 Ksh; in Nyalenda B it was 2.90 Ksh and 3.70 Ksh in Manyatta B.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines urban informal settlement (slum) water service access in Kisumu, Kenya, focusing on shared community water kiosks and master-operator distribution networks serving slum residents too poor to afford individual piped connections.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain wording, the study evaluates an institutional/regulatory utility-community governance model—the Delegated Management Model (DMM) operating under the Kenya Water Act 2002 and WASREB licensing/tariff framework. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, it empirically analyzes concrete rule-type mechanisms directly governing water service access by comparing DMM settlements (Nyalenda A and B) with direct utility contracting (Manyatta B): (1) utility regulatory/contracting structure (delegated bulk-metered master-operator contracts vs. direct utility accounts); (2) administrative burden and connection fee requirements (local slum application processing and meter/pipe-only capital costs vs. repeated trips to distant utility offices and full layout/connection fees); (3) tariff and cost-recovery rules (subsidized bulk utility supply and negotiated retail tariffs vs. unregulated market pricing); and (4) billing enforcement, disconnection rules, and payment accommodation (verbal kiosk payment agreements, nested collective liability, and short-term master-operator payment accommodation vs. direct utility disconnection).
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary mixed-methods empirical data collected in May-June 2013 across three slums in Kisumu, including a random sample survey of 103 water kiosk operators analyzed with descriptive statistics and one-way ANOVA, in-depth key informant interviews with 8 master operators, and direct observation.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports multiple access-relevant outcomes: retail water price per 20-L container (affordability), kiosk connection/start-up capital cost, meter disconnection rates due to bill non-payment, service continuity/reliability disruptions (meter theft, pipe vandalism, daily disruption complaints, and household fallback to unsafe surface/well sources), and participation of women and lower-education operators in service provision.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (water kiosk operators, N = 103 across Nyalenda A n = 47, Nyalenda B n = 26, and Manyatta B n = 30; plus 8 master-operator key informants), exposure (DMM delegated governance vs. direct utility management without DMM), outcomes (retail water prices, connection costs, disconnection incidence, infrastructure disruption), and comparative cross-sectional mixed-methods study design are all clearly identified.

study_design: Comparative cross-sectional mixed-methods study (random sample structured survey with one-way ANOVA across two DMM settlements and one non-DMM control settlement, plus in-depth key informant interviews and participant observation)
population_and_sample: Water kiosk operators in three informal settlements in Kisumu, Kenya (random sample N = 103 interviewed May-June 2013: Nyalenda A n = 47, Nyalenda B n = 26, Manyatta B control slum n = 30) and key informants representing all 8 master operators in Nyalenda A and B
exposure: Delegated Management Model (DMM) utility-community water governance structure (delegated bulk-metered master operators, local application processing, reduced kiosk connection fee requirements, subsidized/negotiated tariffs, and nested collective billing/disconnection rules in Nyalenda A and B) compared with direct utility kiosk contracting without DMM (Manyatta B)
outcome: Retail water price per 20-L container (affordability), kiosk connection/start-up capital cost, meter disconnection due to bill payment problems, infrastructure and service reliability disruptions (meter theft, pipe vandalism, daily customer complaints), and operator socio-demographic inclusion (gender, age, education)
rationale: This empirical mixed-methods comparative study in three informal settlements in Kisumu, Kenya satisfies all inclusion criteria (c1-c6). It examines community water service access via slum water kiosks (c1) and evaluates rule-type legal, administrative, and regulatory mechanisms under the Delegated Management Model versus direct utility management—specifically utility contracting structure, local application administrative burdens and kiosk connection fee rules, subsidized bulk tariffs and negotiated retail water pricing, and non-payment disconnection/accommodation rules (c2, both plain and narrow 2026-10-13 readings). Using a random survey of 103 kiosk operators (one-way ANOVA and descriptive comparisons) and 8 master-operator interviews (c3, c5), it reports concrete access outcomes including retail water prices per 20-L container, connection start-up costs, meter disconnections for non-payment, and service disruptions/reliability (c4), in English (c6). Note that the operator/kiosk unit of analysis should be recorded explicitly at extraction per scope discipline rules.
